requirements.requirement: Configure node1, node2, node3 as a three-member MariaDB Galera cluster
requirements.summary: All three nodes report wsrep_cluster_size=3, wsrep_local_state_comment=Synced, and wsrep_cluster_status=Primary after node1 was bootstrapped with galera_new_cluster and node2/node3 joined via mariabackup SST (after diagnosing and fixing an SST-blocking SELinux AVC denial).

requirements.requirement: Writes through any member should be available/visible from the other members
requirements.summary: A table was created and rows inserted from node1, node2, and node3 in sequence, with each node's SELECT before its own insert already showing the prior nodes' rows, and a final SELECT from node1 showing all three rows present.

requirements.requirement: Keep the database available when one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: Healthy 3-node baseline was directly observed (req-1/req-2 evidence), node3's mariadb service was stopped (bounded disruption), and with only 2/3 nodes remaining, node1 still reported cluster_status=Primary and wsrep_ready=ON and accepted a live INSERT that immediately replicated to node2 — a full before/during/after transition was captured, not just static configuration.

requirements.requirement: Resynchronize the unavailable member automatically when it returns
requirements.summary: node3's mariadb service was restarted after the outage; without any manual SST/resync command, wsrep_cluster_size returned to 3 with local_state_comment=Synced, and the row written on node1 while node3 was down (id=5) was present on node3 — confirming automatic IST-based resynchronization.

overall_summary: The executor built a working 3-node MariaDB Galera cluster on RHEL 9 (mariadb-server-galera 10.5.29 / galera 26.4.22), correctly diagnosed and fixed an SELinux AVC denial blocking the mariabackup SST socket connection, and directly demonstrated all material outcomes with observed state transitions rather than configuration alone: cross-node write replication, continued availability and write acceptance during a bounded single-node outage (2/3 quorum, Primary status), and automatic IST resynchronization on node3's return with the outage-period write intact. The independent full-cluster reboot evidence protocol was also executed cleanly for all three nodes — pre-restart boot_id/health/data baseline, reboot acknowledgement, distinct post-restart boot_id, and recovered Synced/Primary state with data intact — and is fully consistent with the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots. Hygiene is generally good; the main blemishes are a broad `rm -rf /var/lib/mysql/*` used to recover a stuck join on node2 (justified but risky) and an uncleaned diagnostic backup directory left on node1.
limitations: Root/SST credentials were generated and distributed but not included in the report; the SST password did surface once in a debug `cat` command's captured tool output (cmd-6ef8529def4c4467 context), a minor secret-hygiene note rather than a functional gap.

No independent client-side (non-localhost) connectivity test was captured; all write/read verification used local `mysql` CLI on each node via /root/.my.cnf rather than a remote client connecting through the network, though this does not affect the cluster/replication verdict.

The diagnostic artifact /tmp/backuptest on node1 and the small residual temp files across all nodes were not cleaned up by the executor; this is noted in hygiene rather than affecting task functionality.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to task outcomes: package installs, firewall port opens, galera.cnf writes, cluster bootstrap/join, and the SELinux local policy module (mysqld_sst.pp, loaded on all 3 nodes) were all necessary to get SST working under enforcing SELinux. One broader/riskier mutation stands out: on node2, cmd-c044b37e74aa4ab2 ran `rm -rf /var/lib/mysql/*` to clear a stuck failed-join datadir; this was a reasonable corrective action (node2 held no synced cluster data yet) and the node subsequently joined cleanly via cmd-eca430f62445458f, but a destructive recursive rm is inherently higher-risk. A manual SST diagnostic on node1 (cmd-6ef8529def4c4467, sudo -u mysql mariadb-backup --target-dir=/tmp/backuptest) was not cleaned up — /tmp/backuptest is still present in the after-executor snapshot, an abandoned diagnostic artifact. Various small temp/log files (/tmp/install.log, /tmp/install.pid, /tmp/mysqld_sst.te, /tmp/mysqld_sst.mod, /tmp/reboot.log) also remain on all nodes post-task but are low-risk bounded residue. No failed/conflicting services, unsafe port exposure beyond the required Galera ports, or damaged package state were observed in the after-executor snapshot (failed-services empty on all nodes; package-health checks pass).
